title: WHY ALMOST NOBODY LIVES ON THE CANADIAN SHIELD
description:
Half of Canada is almost empty, and the reason is under your feet: a horseshoe of rock billions of years old wrapped around Hudson Bay. Here's how the Canadian Shield decides where Canadians live, and why the emptiest land in the country is also some of the richest.

In August 1883, a CPR blacksmith named Tom Flanagan stopped beside a freshly blasted railway cut north of Lake Huron and noticed rust-coloured rock. Months later, the land was bought for 1 dollar an acre. What he was really looking at is the last thing this story answers.

The Canadian Shield covers about 5 million km², roughly half of Canada. It holds some of the oldest dated rock on Earth: the Acasta Gneiss at about 4.03 billion years, and the Nuvvuagittuq belt in Quebec, dated in 2025 to about 4.16 billion years, a figure scientists still argue over. You'll see how ancient cratons collided into mountains that may have rivalled the Himalayas, how they wore down to their roots, and how an ice sheet 3 to 4 km thick scraped the land down to bare stone.

Then the hard part: why farming fails up here, what happened when Canada sent settlers and veterans into the Great Clay Belt, how Cree and Anishinaabe peoples lived across the Shield by canoe and portage, and why muskeg swallowed CPR track, railcars and hundreds of carloads of gravel, at a cost of up to 700,000 dollars for a single mile by one estimate.

Finally, the reward: the Porcupine Gold Rush of 1909, Athabasca uranium about 100 times richer than the world average, diamonds found in 1991 by following a glacier's trail, Flin Flon, 237,000 tonnes of arsenic frozen under Yellowknife, and the Ring of Fire, where Ottawa promised 1 billion dollars for roads on October 21, 2026.
